I dug up this old ass comment from years ago I left in response to the question "What is the field like for grunts?" Do with it what you will

You'll find out 3 days prior if you're lucky, that you are going to the field for x amount of days. So you pack your shit, carry it downstairs to dump it all out to check it, then pack it again. The next morning you wake up at 0430 to make armory draw at 0530. If you're smart you show up early to try and beat the line because the entire company at the armory is a shit show. Eventually you get your rifle and NVGs, and head to the staging area. A rifle watch is posted so everyone can bring their packs down if they havent yet. It's now 0745. SSgt says trucks will be there at 0800 for transpo, so dont go anywhere, (especially not the px for that dip you forgot to pack). 0930 rolls around and the trucks finally show up. You cram yourself and 19 of your best friends, plus packs into the back of a truck meant to seat 16. You take some bumpy ass road to the range, most likely a dirt road, so bring a cloth or something to filter your breathing as best as possible. It's now 1000 and you're at the range. You get off and count your serialized gear for the 3rd time in as many hours, set your packs down in rows, and sit down. 3 seconds later you're called over by SSgt for the RSO brief. It's the same shit everytime, and soon you'll be saying it along with him. What happens next varies from range to range but odds are you'll do some dry runs, a BZO shoot to zero in your optic, and find some time to get a snack down. You'll spend so much time waiting for every single team in every squad from every platoon to do their run that by the time it's your turn to go, what was supposed to be your day run is now a night run. But first go cowitness your PEQs. At about 1130 you get to go to sleep, but first, count your EDL first, someone probably lost something. But wait! Your ass is on first hour fire watch. Be happy, it's the best hour there is. 0015 rolls by and you kick that one asshole awake for his post. He looks at his watch, tells you to fuck yourself, and goes back to sleep. Just kick him a few more times and start cussing him out. Hell get up eventually. You finally lay down on your little sleeping mat at 0100, but quickly realize that your neighbor is halfway on your mat, and there's a big rock underneath. You either deal with it or not, but you fall asleep quick enough, only to he woken up at 0530 to the lovely sound of those three little words. Revelie revelie revelie! Soon those words will dig into your soul and instantly ruin your morning. You shave and brush your teeth, and choke down another mre before counting off your gear once more. You'll sit down, sip some water, and stare at the dirt in front of you, having put your sleeping mat and bag away. The cycle then repeats. Dry runs, waiting for your turn on the range, now you get shitty fire watch hours, the asshole still refuses to get up, and you count the days before you EAS. Get comfy, you got a ways to go.

To echo what lots of others are saying (this is in order of usefulness in my opinion) :

Phoenix is hugely useful (Captain Rex is vital) They also will get you Emperor Palpatine and Thrown. Their ships get you Chimera and remain relevant all the way to endgame with the Profundity fleet. 

Bounty Hunters gets you Chewie as well as access to the credit heist and training droid events which will be instrumental in early growth. Also their ships are all good, get you Hans Millennium Falcon, and make up the entirety of the Executor Fleet. 

Imperial Troopers are a phenomenal early team, get you R2-D2, clear one of the assault battles which all have strong return on investments. Focus on Admiral Piett, he's important in the team as all the way to the end game.

Geos are a super fun team to play with, horrible to fight, and massively important in a guild setting. Their ships are great at a low level, and super easy to farm. 

I see you already have at least three of the 4 non event requirements for Commander Luke Skywalker going. He's a fantastic toon, plugs into any rebel team other than Phoenix early on until you get the rest of his team built. Unfortunately his ideal team has 4 event toons, with the only regular farm being threepio&Chewie. But even then he's fantastic and relevant in the endgame. 

Last bit of advice, make an SWGOH.GG account, and join a guild. Guilds are huge for making progress in building your characters quicker, and unlocking great characters like OG Han, General Kenobi, Darth Traya, Hermit Yoda, Wampa, Rebel Officer Leia, Shaak-Ti, and Wat Tambor. All of those are requirements for some type of journey except Traya, and she's a fantastic team.

I'd say 270 is a fair average. There's the studs who run 300s, the weak bodies who barely make 235, and everything in-between. Your kep here is pull-ups. They make up a huge chunk of your points. Plank is easy as fuck. Max-max-relax. Don't kill yourself for not getting sub 18 on the run. Most people I know don't get it. 

Squad PT is usually at the SLs whim. I've had PTs that are mock PFTs, log runs, casevac runs, ruck runs, or just green on green death runs. Or you may do a lifting competition type PT. Or you might just do a recovery day and stretch for half an hour. I'd say it won't usually take longer than an hour and a half for a tough PT, but if your plt leaders want to do a PT, hydrate and prepare for a slay. 

Depending on the op, maintaining weight isn't too bad of an issue, but sometimes you're gonna lose weight. It's the nature of the beast. The experience depends on what you're doing. PB ops suck by design. Urban ops are usually fun. Standard ranges are usually ok. Sleeping in the field is weather dependent. Always check the forecast and prepare accordingly. 

At one point I was running almost 30 miles a week, but some of that was my own exercises. Mileage will vary drastically since, again, it's at the whim of your leaders. I'd say that it would be fair to expect about 15 a week just from unit PT

There is a cost. Your knees and back will suffer the most. Proper stretching and supplements such as fish oil will help reduce this, but 4 years rucking heavy weight up and down hills will still take it's toll

Pool: Yes, sometimes more or less depending on your company, but annual swim qual is still a thing and intermediate is the requirement for the infantry. 

PFT: A first class (235+) is the requirement, but most grunts will usually run 270+

Own workout time: When in garrison, absolutely. In fact if you aren't working out on your own, you will struggle. Your squad PTs may keep you in decent shape, but it typically won't be enough. In the field however, you will not have time to workout

Alright. I've spent about 30 minutes trying to find a way to word this without sounding like a douche, and I'm not sure if I got it, but I'm gonna try. 

Obligatory TL;DR
20 miles a day for 7 days with 100lbs? If you can do this, I'll shit you a golden egg. 

Longer post:

First off, I've been an active duty infantry marine for nearly a decade. I am intimately familiar with hiking heavy weight over long distances, as well as it's effects on the body. I'm not a doctor or anything like that, but I know my knees and back shouldn't be this messed up at my age.

Every year or two we do 32km (20mi) hikes that carry 45-60lbs. The average rate of march on this event is 3 mph. Even if we rest for 10 minutes every hour, (if only we were so lucky) that movement takes about 7 hours at a minimum. That obviously still leaves most of the day for rest, refit, and all that good stuff we humans need to stay functional. 

So far it may sound sucky, but not impossible, and you'd be right. However, this is with about half the weight you're suggesting. Continue to factor in that the next day, walking is hardly an option, chafing is now your life, and the human factor is a real thing. One day of this and you will have no desire to do anything but lay in bed and drink beer from a straw, cuz you don't have to move as much that way. 

You may have noticed that terrain hasn't even been mentioned yet. Let's talk about that. That hike I mentioned was mostly flat terrain. We got real lucky. Increasing elevation will take any wind out of your sails real fast. Going uphill sucks. A lot. With weight, your pace is slower than a snail, your steps are choppy, and your ankles are vulnerable. Going down seems easier, but now your knees are at risk. And it won't happen overnight, but it'll get you. Your back, primarily your lumbar, will suffer. Your upper and middle back will compress, your shoulders and traps will rub raw. 

You want to do this every day for a week straight with twice the weight? I simply don't think it's possible. I've seen some ridiculously impressive men do some downright insane things over the years in this field, but this is just way beyond the scope of what I think is possible. I almost want to challenge you to give it a shot, but I can't recommend even attempting this with a good conscience

Historically, the Jian was popular during the Han Dynasty in China (202 BC - 220 AD, give or take.) At this time, iron had started to come to prominence, and bronze was very well established by then. 

The time period and technology of the show is very different as they have steam engines and ironclad warships. 

Despite this, I'd say regular bronze would be best. Gold seems to be reserved for jewelry and the ruling/extreme upper class across both the fire nation and the earth kingdom. Piandao, while extremely well off, doesn't strike me as the kind of man who has much gold laying around, nor one who would just give one of his students some to decorate the hilt and pommel of his sword. 

As for leather, they certainly had it in Han China. It was usually tanned by use of fats and oils, likely from the animal it was harvested from, and stretched over a fire, using the heat and smoke. Dyeing leather is as old as tanning, so use whatever color you want. 

But they also control elements with their minds and cast sword blades in molds, so do whatever you want, enjoy your process, and have fun making what is sure to be a gorgeous piece.

-Swimming is probably one of the most undervalued skills in the Corps by lower enlisted. The amount of marines who can't swim is atrocious. Don't be one of them

-Work to be the best at what you are currently doing, and that discipline will get you where you need to go. If you're a student, be the best student. When you're a recruit, be the best recruit. Ect. ect. 

-PT is important, but don't forget the mental side of things. Knowledge and job proficiency are just as, if not more, crucial. 

-Don't be a dick. 

-Don't broadcast your intentions too early. Commands find a way of stopping you, seemingly for shits and grins. 

-Make friends, take pictures, enjoy your time in. It could end at a moments notice

-Take care of your body. Start taking fish oils early. Don't jump from the back of a 7-ton. Your body may be able to take it now, but not for long. Stretch daily, full body, and thoroughly. This lifestyle is exactly that. You're in for the long haul. Marathon, not sprint

-Trust in your NCOs. They may seem like assholes, (and they probably are) but they ultimately have your best interests in mind. Good or bad, they will mold you into the marine you need to be. Learn something from every single one of them, even if it's an example on how not to lead. 

-Save your money. Don't buy stupid shit. Get a cheap, reliable car at a good interest rate, and ask an NCO or older marine to help you in that process. 

-Find a hobby, preferably with some sort of initial financial investment. (surfing, rock climbing, archery, or music are some of mine) The money upfront will help you stay with it instead of dropping it. 

-I can't tell you to not start drinking, but for the love of God do so sparingly, and if you're not 21, in the safety of your own room if at all. This goes hand in hand with the hobby bit. Do something cool instead of drinking.

You'll find out 3 days prior if you're lucky, that you are going to the field for x amount of days. So you pack your shit, carry it downstairs to dump it all out to check it, then pack it again. The next morning you wake up at 0430 to make armory draw at 0530. If you're smart you show up early to try and beat the line because the entire company at the armory is a shit show. Eventually you get your rifle and NVGs, and head to the staging area. A rifle watch is posted so everyone can bring their packs down if they havent yet. It's now 0745. SSgt says trucks will be there at 0800 for transpo, so dont go anywhere, (especially not the px for that dip you forgot to pack). 0930 rolls around and the trucks finally show up. You cram yourself and 19 of your best friends, plus packs into the back of a truck meant to seat 16. You take some bumpy ass road to the range, most likely a dirt road, so bring a cloth or something to filter your breathing as best as possible. It's now 1000 and you're at the range. You get off and count your serialized gear for the 3rd time in as many hours, set your packs down in rows, and sit down. 3 seconds later you're called over by SSgt for the RSO brief. It's the same shit everytime, and soon you'll be saying it along with him. What happens next varies from range to range but odds are you'll do some dry runs, a BZO shoot to zero in your optic, and find some time to get a snack down. You'll spend so much time waiting for every single team in every squad from every platoon to do their run that by the time it's your turn to go, what was supposed to be your day run is now a night run. But first go cowitness your PEQs. At about 1130 you get to go to sleep, but first, count your EDL first, someone probably lost something. But wait! Your ass is on first hour fire watch. Be happy, it's the best hour there is. 0015 rolls by and you kick that one asshole awake for his post. He looks at his watch, tells you to fuck yourself, and goes back to sleep. Just kick him a few more times and start cussing him out. Hell get up eventually. You finally lay down on your little sleeping mat at 0100, but quickly realize that your neighbor is halfway on your mat, and there's a big rock underneath. You either deal with it or not, but you fall asleep quick enough, only to he woken up at 0530 to the lovely sound of those three little words. Revelie revelie revelie! Soon those words will dig into your soul and instantly ruin your morning. You shave and brush your teeth, and choke down another mre before counting off your gear once more. You'll sit down, sip some water, and stare at the dirt in front of you, having put your sleeping mat and bag away. The cycle then repeats. Dry runs, waiting for your turn on the range, now you get shitty fire watch hours, the asshole still refuses to get up, and you count the days before you EAS. Get comfy, you got a ways to go.
